extracted.intended_audience: writers of short periodical essays and readers interested in the aims and methods of essay-writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing single-sheet/periodical essays: be concise, lively, self-contained, and aimed to instruct or amuse a broad reading public. Also includes standards for compiling natural-history species accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form-dependent reader expectations (volume vs separate papers)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man who publishes his Works in a Volume, has an infinite Advantage over one who communicates his Writings to the World in loose Tracts and single Pieces. We do not expect to meet with any thing in a bulky Volume, till after some heavy Preamble, and several Words of Course, to prepare the Reader for what follows: Nay, Authors have established it as a kind of Rule, that a Man ought to be dull sometimes; as the most severe Reader makes Allowances for many Rests and Nodding-places in a Voluminous Writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volumes afford allowances for digressions, preambles, and occasional dullness; by contrast, separate sheets/periodical papers cannot rely on that indulgence and must engage immediately. Treat this choice of form as setting expectations for pacing, density, and tolerance of filler material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and immediacy for single-sheet essays
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who publish their Thoughts in distinct Sheets, and as it were by Piece-meal, have none of these Advantages. We must immediately fall into our Subject, and treat every Part of it in a lively Manner, or our Papers are thrown by as dull and insipid: Our Matter must lie close together, and either be wholly new in itself, or in the Turn it receives from our Expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin promptly on the subject; keep language lively; pack matter tightly; favour novelty either of subject-matter or of expression. Avoid long preambles — a periodical essay must be engaging from the outset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-containedness: each paper should 'make out' what it lacks in bulk
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often expected that every Sheet should be a kind of Treatise, and make out in Thought what it wants in Bulk: That a Point of Humour should be worked up in all its Parts; and a Subject touched upon in its most essential Articles, without the Repetitions, Tautologies and Enlargements, that are indulged to longer Labours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each essay, though short, treats its point thoroughly: develop the humour or moral fully within the small space, cover essential aspects, and avoid reliance on repetition or expansion that longer works may use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chymical method (potency over quantity)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Essay-Writer must practise in the Chymical Method, and give the Virtue of a full Draught in a few Drops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for concentrated effect: produce the intellectual or comic 'virtue' of a long discourse in a brief, potent form. Prioritise intensity and precision of thought and expression over sheer length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aims and public purpose of periodical essays
rubrics_metrics.description: Our common Prints would be of great Use were they thus calculated to diffuse good Sense through the Bulk of a People, to clear up their Understandings, animate their Minds with Virtue, dissipate the Sorrows of a heavy Heart, or unbend the Mind from its more severe Employments with innocent Amusements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write with the public benefit in mind: instruct, promote virtue, console, or provide harmless entertainment. The moral and social utility of essays is a central standard of worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience selection and realistic expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: I am not at all mortified, when sometimes I see my Works thrown aside by Men of no Taste nor Learning... To these I must apply the Fable of the Mole... It is not therefore for the Benefit of Moles that I publish these my daily Essays. But besides such as are Moles through Ignorance, there are others who are Moles through Envy... one Author is a Mole to another Author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise different reader types: some readers won't appreciate the essays due to ignorance or envy. Target the receptive public (those of 'best Sense') and accept that certain audiences will not reward or understand the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural history account: required elements for a species monograph
rubrics_metrics.description: If the several Writers among them took each his particular Species, and gave us a distinct Account of its Original, Birth and Education; its Policies, Hostilities and Alliances, with the Frame and Texture of its inward and outward Parts, and particularly those that distinguish it from all other Animals, with their peculiar Aptitudes for the State of Being in which Providence has placed them, it would be one of the best Services their Studies could do Mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good species account should cover origin, birth and upbringing, social/predatory relationships (policies, hostilities, alliances), anatomy (inward and outward texture), distinguishing features, and ecological/functional aptitudes. Compile based on books and observations; acknowledge observational limits (seas/deserts/microscopic species) and infer unknowns by analogy where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral indicators of instinct for observational natural history
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances to note: the Hen providing a nest in unfrequented places; turning eggs frequently so all parts partake of vital Warmth; punctual return before eggs cool; seasonal variation in attendance; helping the chick to break its Prison; covering from weather; teaching to help itself; abandoning the nest after usual time or if young do not appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing animal instinct, emphasise observable, repeatable behaviours (nest choice, egg-tending routines, feeding/teaching, seasonal adjustments, responses to confinement) as evidence. Use such concrete instances to distinguish instinctual actions from reasoned behaviour.
